paragraphs.text: Capítulo 2. Exercise

I got really lucky with learning about exercise, and enjoying exercise—but only because I got unlucky first. Like most kids in my town, I swam and played soccer, but unlike most I got really into skateboarding. I was decent enough at those other activities, but I loved skateboarding best. It felt the most liberating because I could do it any time of day or night, and I loved that there was no oficial court or playing field—city streets, curbs, benches, and stairs were as varied as they come. And it was transportation too, so it offered all sorts of possibilities for adventure. I could do it alone or with others, and I loved that you could innovate by making up new tricks. The sport was Still relatively small at the time (this was the late 1980s and early 1990s) and, as I mentioned in the introduction to this book, several of my friends turned professional just out of high school. Not me. I kept getting hurt. By the time I was a sophomore, I had broken the same foot twice and messed up the arches ofmy feet. And that's how exercise came into my life. Luckily, a supportive physical education teacher named Bob Peters noticed how often I arrived to Class on crutches and pointed me toward a small weight room near the pool. No one really used it except the football team, and that was only during the summer months. So in many ways, it was a perfect situation. I could go in there and use the equipment whenever I wanted and I didn't have to compare my (lack of) strength to anyone else because I was mostly alone. Although I didn't realize it at the time, the dearth of other people weight training also saved me from the terrible, often dangerous advice people tend to give others in gyms. The only problem was that I had absolutely no idea what I was doing. There were anatomy charts of muscles and bones and tendons on the walls, and a few diagrams of exercises that were easy enough to follow, but nothing else. That drove me to the library and local bookstore, where I read about weight training. Which left me even more confused. The recommendations were all over the place. "Do one set per body part but super slow." "Do twenty sets per body part." "Train for thirty minutes maximum, three times a week." "Train for two hours, twice a day, Six days per week," and on and on. It was dizzying. I completely empathize with people who experience immense confusion when they try to figure out how best to exercise, because I felt that too. Luckily (again), one of the books I stumbled upon was by Arthur Jones, the inventor of Nautilus exercise machines. Jones was a proponent of doing short, intense workouts two to three times per week, or even less. While that didn't sound like enough to get results, I liked that he had a rationale for his suggestions and I liked that his general training philosophy was based on science—in particular the work of physiologist Hans Selye, who studied stress and adaptations to stress.J (More about Selye in the next chapter.. Exercise, Jones pointed out, is a form of stress that the body adjusts to with both specific adaptations, which reflect the type of stress that had been imposed to create them, and message, and Mike called me back. I was sixteen at the time, and my mother was understandably worried. She wondered: Who was this grown man calling her teenage son at home? Apparently, Mike appreciated that when I called him, I rattled off a quick list of questions onto his answering machine that made it Clear I had read Jones's books. We ended up speaking for several hours over the course of a few months about weight training, fitness more generally, and science— both actual science and scientists. It wasn't as if he gently took me under his Wing though. Mike was super intense. He would sort of bark at me when he spoke, but there was always a hint of kindness in his delivery. And he did charge me $ 150 for the calls, which was most of my savings at the time but it was well worth it. I'm telling you this story because what I learned from those calls with Mike has stayed with me and I credit much of my regular progress with resistance training over the last thirty years to him. Here are ten counsels Mike gave me that I never forgot and always strive to implement with respect to resistance training. 1 After warming up, do not train for much more than Sixty to seventy-five minutes at a time... you'll progress much faster that way. Occasionally your training may go longer if you are waiting for equipment at a gym, but that's just about the only reason to extend a session much beyond seventy-five minutes. 2 Always strive to use good form, meaning use a full range of motion for every repetition of every set, and control the weight from start to finish.

3 Learn to use resistance as a tool to stress the muscles you're trying to train. Focus as you do the lift to feel the muscles you're trying to train working. Mike added: If you can't feel the muscle you're trying to target you'll want to use "pre-exhaustion" techniques when you train. I explain what pre-exhaustion is later, but as the name suggests, it involves doing an isolation exercise (where only one joint moves) immediately before you do a compound exercise (where multiple joints move) for the same muscle. Mike knew most people hate doing pre-exhaustion exercises because they require using less weight on the compound movement. But for getting results with otherwise hard-to-feel and Slowto-progress muscles, he was spot on. 4 If you're new to resistance training, you'll benefit greatly by taking one to three weeks to find the right movements that collectively allow you to target all the major muscles of your body and that work best for your body mechanics. Learn to execute those movements correctly using relatively light (for you) weights, meaning an amount of resistance where you can do ten to twelve repetitions, even though you could easily do five more. This one-to-three-week "break-in" period is about learning how to train before you start the real work. Ifyou've been regularly training with weights for a while, I suggest you take a full week off. Stay out of the gym completely for seven, or even up to ten, days. You may feel like you're standing Still during this period but it's critical to your long-term progress, and you'll thank me later. Once you start your real workouts, it doesn't take many sets per muscle group to get the results you want, IF you do them with proper form... and intensity. 5 Intensity is defined as working with a weight that is heavy enough (for you) that it limits you to completing Six to twelve repetitions maximum in good form. There are times to deliberately use heavier weights that limit you to three to five repetitions maximum, or lighter weights that permit you to do thirteen to twenty repetitions maximum. When and where to do that comes later. If you're not familiar with any of these terms, don't worry. 1'11 get into all this as the chapter unfolds. But what struck me looking back on these notes as I wrote this chapter is how many sets and exercises to do, and how often to train, was debated like crazy back then and it Still is now. Mike was a bit extreme; he favored doing very few actual work sets of an exercise—meaning effortful sets, not warm-ups. In fact, he suggested doing even just one work set per exercise, and one to two exercises per muscle group. I Will address the science-supported and practical reasons for doing a bit more than that later. But for now, let's take in Mike's points about a relatively low number of work sets, or what is referred to as a volume of sets. Because one thing most everyone agrees on now that Mike extolled is this: If done properly, you don't need a high volume of sets per exercise or muscle group, and that more is often counterproductive.

And sometimes you have to push past failure by getting assistance from a training partner who nudges the weight just a bit, or by immediately reducing the weight and doing two to three more repetitions until you hit failure again. 9 Learn to enjoy training hard. Don't socialize in the gym. Warm up, train, and get out! And undoubtedly the best and most classic Mentzer-ism of all: 10 "DO NOT LISTEN TO WHAT ANYONE ELSE TELLS YOU AS MOST PEOPLE WHO LIFT WEIGHTS ARE MORONS AND MOST OF WHAT THEY DO AND SAY IS TOTAL BS!" (Mike literally yelled number 10 into the Phone so loud that I winced and had to move the receiver away from my ear. Later I understood what words of wisdom and care those were. To be fair, there are many folks in the fitness education and training community who Offer great advice, but Mike wasn't terribly off with this one.) However coarse the delivery, those ten points were (and remain) gems that we can all benefit from. Again, as I said, I got lucky. We now have tons of peer-reviewed science to support the general logic of Mike's advice, although at the time, much of it ran countercurrent to the dominant views about resistance training, most notably the popular idea at the time that "more volume is better." As it turns out, quality reps and sets are what count, and it does not take much high-quality resistance training to trigger the specific adaptations Jones outlined in his book. (Note: Quality has many meanings, which we Will cover repeatedly below.) Of course, those ten points do not exhaustively cover all one needs to know about resistance training, and considering the results of studies that have been done since, there are some important caveats that 1'11 address. What I can say, however, is that I took Mike's general advice to heart. After our first call, I took a full week off from any resistance training and then, even though I had been lifting for about Six months, I devoted a few weeks to finding the free-weight, weight-machine, and body-weight-only exercises that worked best for me—meaning the ones I could do for full range of motion, pain free, and that allowed me to stress each of the major muscle groups. I found the right combination of compound (multi-joint) exercises and isolation (single-joint) exercises for each muscle group, like the shoulders, biceps, quadriceps, et cetera. Then I started doing resistance training three times per week, training different muscles on each of those three days: calves and legs one day, then a day or two off, then chest, back, and abdominals (and neck), then a day off, then shoulders and arms, another day off, and then back to calves and legs day. So again, three days total in the gym per week. I've done that body part—split pretty much consistently for thirty-five years now. Even if I am traveling, I find a gym to do these workouts. And if I go to a location where I can't find a gym, 1'11 do body-weightonly exercises, or I take the week off and stay active in other ways. While general activity is no substitute for resistance training, I have found that a week off approximately every four months can be beneficial. I can arrange it to happen during a vacation or other travel, or if I get sick— fortunately a rarity for me—l don't train. I rest up and stay out of the gym (and thus avoid getting others sick too!) and that becomes the week off. Approaching resistance training this way has allowed me to make consistent progress with about three hours per week of resistance training while Still fully enjoying other aspects oflife and avoiding injuries. Before going any further I want to acknowledge something that Mike got somewhat wrong and that is important to highlight here. There is not one best way to resistance train! You won't find too many effective programs that recommend fewer than three days of resistance training per week, but there are some good ones that involve more days. Some programs, like the one described in this book, are based on a body part split in which you train different body parts on different days. And even those splits can vary. For instance some people like to train all their pushing muscles of the upper body (chest, shoulders, triceps) on one day, and pulling muscles (back and biceps) on another day, and then legs a different day. Other programs have you train your whole body in every workout; others Still alternate between upper and lower body workouts. All these can work. Below I explain the rationale for the split I use and suggest—because it offers some not-soobvious benefits. The point stands, nonetheless, that there are a lot of ways to resistance train. Yet there is a core set of principles upon which all people—women, men, inexperienced, experienced, young, old—must rely on to build an effective program. I define an "effective program" as one that people are likely to Stick to over many years, and that works well for those also doing cardiovascular exercise, which we know is also vital to our health and provides distinct benefits from resistance training. Many people want to grow certain muscles and leave others as they are. Others want to grow all their muscles. An effective program should Offer all those options too. It also means a program that does not sap your energy but instead gives you more energy. After all, what good is a program that leaves you tired and hungry to an extent that inhibits your work and relationships? While it is normal (and reflective of an effective workout) to be tired after a training session, that fatigue should be somewhat transient, even that day. Your workout shouldn't leave you dragging. During your work sets, you work hard—both mentally and physically—and you'll sweat and perhaps get a bit sore, but those are not the goal. Those are the by-products of quality workouts. You also want to Still be able to think and walk (!) in the hours and days that follow. I've come up with a template to help everyone. It's part of Why I call it a foundational fitness program—so named because it's grounded in research, the ideas above and that follow below, and the core physiological principles that undergird all effective programs. These principles Will never change because they reflect the mechanisms by which muscles, bones, and connective tissues get stronger and, if desired, grow larger. If you make sure that your resistance training follows this template, you can Still tailor it to your goals, body type, schedule, and the I also noticed that I always felt better mentally when I did a mix of cardiovascular and resistance training across the week, as opposed to just one or the other. I thought perhaps it was the fresh air... but I noticed this even if it was raining and I was forced to run on a treadmill. I should mention that this was the early 1990s, and the ideologies within different sports and sectors of the fitness world were Still very siloed. Today, we believe that being stronger helps in pretty much every sport and physical activity. Back then people also thought that if you did resistance training and then stopped, your muscles would turn to fat. Today we know that is false—in fact, it's impossible. Nowadays, most every serious athlete resistance trains during both the main and the offseason. And we now know that even if you don't play a sport, if your goal is to be healthy and fit, and to stay uninjured, and live as long as possible, and to do so with vigor, you're best off doing a combination of both resistance training and cardiovascular training. This is true for women and for men. We also know that what defines an effective resistance training program is the same for women and men, such as the need for intensity—training to failure on work sets (or close to failure)—as well as proper form, allowing suficient rest between workouts for specific adaptations to occur, and more. As Lauren Colenso-Semple, a PhD in integrative physiology and a strength and conditioning coach, and one of the world's leading experts in strength and hypertrophy training, stated so clearly (and adamantly) when she was a guest on my podcast, all the data point to the fact that when it comes to resistance training to improve strength and/or muscle size, the same principles and techniques apply to women and to men— including the need to train to failure or very close to it.4 Looking back, for me it was thanks to those repeated foot injuries from skateboarding, the generosity of a physical education teacher, a few good books, some formative calls with one of the world's experts in resistance training, and being a naiVe, lovestruck teenager that I learned early on how to get in and stay in great all-around shape. Lucky indeed. And I promise you: If you follow the template here and add in cardiovascular training, too, you can get into and stay in great all-around shape at any age. Yes, nutrition matters but making exercise part of your life Will absolutely make you a much healthier person, mentally and physically. In this chapter I teach you how to do that. And if you already have a fitness program, I'm confident you'll Still glean a ton of new knowledge that you can use from these pages. Most people exercise because they want to feel and look good in their body. They also want longevity—not just to live as long as possible, but to be capable of doing any number of practical things without pain and, ideally, with relative ease. For example, having enough endurance for a long hike with a backpack. Being strong enough to lift boxes of books or help move furniture. Fast enough to sprint for (and catch) a plane or train without tearing a muscle. Able to open a jar when asked. The protocols here Will enable you to do all that. They Will also help you achieve the body composition (ie., lean tissue-to-fat ratio) you want, while Still allowing you to eat well, and feel more vital. Exercise is extremely potent medicine and, as with sleep, it's one of the best investments you can make toward your mental and physical health. The benefits start from the minute you begin each workout. If all this gives the impression I love exercise. I do, on some days. Training is definitely a pleasure for me, especially if I've slept well, I'm hydrated, I'm caffeinated, and if there's no big stressor weighing on mes That's a lot of ifs, so it won't surprise you that those conditions are often hard to achieve because, well, life happens. I too sometimes get less-than-optimal sleep. I too have a full schedule. I too experience stress. I've had lapses due to the occasional cold. It happens to all of us. That said, really understanding how exercise works and how much good can come from a few hours a week of focused training can keep us on the journey to get and stay fit when we are not feeling motivated. I look forward to workouts because I know that the way I'm training works. That is priceless. Especially for people who don't like exercise, but like the feeling of having done it, knowing your time was well spent—that it Will get you results—is a game changer. In fact, a really good program of the sort I describe here can allow you to make progress most every single week. I mentioned earlier in this introduction that I empathize with people who experience immense confusion when they try to figure out how best to exercise, because I felt that too. So perhaps you're wondering: Why not just discuss "the best way to exercise" here? Maybe you're sensing a pattern: Just like there's no "best" way to resistance train, there's no best way to exercise. We know that resistance training is key. So physician named Susruta, who lived around 600 BCE, was one of the first known practitioners to prescribe exercise. "It should be taken every day," he wrote. "Diseases fly from the presence of a person habituated to regular physical exercise." Susruta's words are as relevant today as they were during his lifetime. The problem is how to implement the prescription. Many people don't do it, or they do it wrong and end up discouraged, injured, or both. So many times I hear people say, "I used to work out every day," or "I used to be so fit," or "I don't have the time or energy to exercise anymore." What is rarely discussed is that exercise, done correctly, gives you energy. It extends your life (ie., gives you more time). It also increases your level of focus for many hours afterward, which also saves you time. And there's more. Research shows that regular exercise can be as or even more effective for improving mood and lowering anxiety than prescription antidepressants or talk therapy. On, and on, and on. Exercise is not a cure-all, but it is often a way to address many of the physical and mental health issues people struggle with. It's just that, as a species, we have not quite come to understand how potent a medicine exercise really is. Then there are those who exercise consistently but overdo one type or just focus on their favorite sport, like running or tennis, Pilates or spin class, and miss out on the very real health benefits that come from variety. In my experience, very few people know how to get in great all-around shape properly. Even fewer stay there. The good news is that doing so is pretty simple, again, once you know how.

It comes in three basic varieties: resistance training, cardiovascular exercise, and mobility and/or flexibility. Resistance exercise is where you use some weight—your body weight, weight machines, or free weights—to challenge your neuromuscular system and connective tissues. Resistance training also strengthens your bones. The hallmark of classic cardiovascular exercise is an increased heart rate for at least twelve minutes and up to seventy-five minutes—or in some cases even longer. There are arguments to be made that one can get effective cardiovascular workouts in shorter bouts of activity, through what's often called high-intensity interval training (HIIT). But we Will return to that nuance later. Finally, mobility and flexibility challenges our ability to stably shift between different bodily positions, and to have access to a full range of functional motion if we need it for athletics or simply in everyday life. If you're now thinking "So I have to do three types of exercise? I barely have time for one!" don't despair. Although it can be great to have mobility and flexibility practice, as I describe later in this chapter, you can see meaningful benefits from protocols that take very little time to complete, in one case just five minutes. And the resistance and cardiovascular sessions I describe below are aimed to give you the maximum benefits for time spent. What is the goal of exercise? Believe it or not, the most important thing to understand about exercise is Why you're doing it. I don't mean your psychology here. I am referring to what you are trying to achieve with each workout; Why you are doing specifically what you are doing. It ensures every workout leads you to achieve your goals. For all that has been written and said about exercise, it often misses this crucial point. All effective forms of exercise share a common purpose: to trigger a set of specific and general adaptations in your body and brain. Exercise is the stimulus, and the general and specific adaptations are your body's response to the stimulus. Exercise can also drive aesthetic changes, like fat loss, or improve sports performance, but those are secondary. "Wait!" I hear you saying, "I exercise to stay fit. Just tell me how to do that." I Will, but I promise you Will accomplish your goals much faster, and you Will make consistent progress, if you understand exercise in this stimulus-adaptation context. Here's an example of how specific adaptations work. Let's say you run or cycle at a moderate pace for thirty minutes. I'm talking about a pace where you can barely hold a conversation without gasping for air. While you do this your heart rate and blood pressure Will rise substantially, you'll breathe more rapidly, you'll sweat, your muscles probably Will burn a bit, and your immune system Will release a bunch of proinflammatory molecules such as interleukin-6 into your blood.8 Sounds terrible, right? Wrong. This constellation of responses—what we call the exercise-induced stress response—will lead to a set of adaptations that directly reflect the stress you just experienced but in the opposite direction. Thousands of coordinated, metabolic, molecular and even genetic changes occur when we exercise—a "molecular choreography," as one group of researchers has put it.2 After doing this for some time, your resting heart rate, blood pressure, and circulating levels of inflammatory molecules Will be lower than they were before you set out on that run. When most people think about what they accomplished by exercising, they tend to think about the calories burned or the mood enhancement it provides in the hours that follow. That's all well and good, but the real magic of exercise resides in the specific and general adaptations it produces. Those are the real "gains" of exercise. They last for days and they compound over time. They literally change your body and brain, and do so in ways that reflect the stress you experienced during the workout. That makes you a physiologically different person —capable of more in every area of life related to the exercise-induced adaptations—stronger, and faster, with more vigor and endurance, and more capable all around. Once you understand and experience the stimulus-adaptation process, you come to understand what effective effort is and when to rest to glean the adaptations you worked to trigger. It can make you wiser too. In fact, as we Will cover later in chapter 6— neuroplasticity, or your ability to learn and rewire your brain—follows the same general contour of "failures" (from genuine efforts to do something!) prompted by specific adaptations that Will help you overcome those "failures" in the near future. The effects of quality exercise on your ability to learn extend way beyond just metaphor. Exercise can directly facilitate neuroplasticity by allowing it to occur.JO Like heat makes metal pliable, so too exercise brings the brain into a state where new neural connections in the brain Young sea squirts swim freely until they are fully grown. The adults then Stick themselves onto a rock and become filter feeders, catching whatever happens to float by. When this transition from swimming to sedentary occurs, sea squirts eat their own brains, leaving only what is necessary for their new passive Style of feeding. Llinás's story about a distantly related animal is relevant to us for two reasons. First, it provides a warning to humans with an overly sedentary lifestyle. As humans age and become less mobile, their brains degenerate too, albeit not as dramatically as does the sea squirt brainl Second, people who continue to exercise—in particular those who do exercise that is challenging (but safe) for them, offset much of typical age-related brain loss that is otherwise observed. This has real implications, allowing them to maintain youthful cognitive function well into their later years, possibly through neurogenesis, the addition of new brain neurons.J5 Deliberate, repetitive, effortful movements that elicit the short-term stress responses (discussed throughout this chapter) trigger a battery of chemical and neural feedback signals to the brain, which both supports the existing brain cells and the connections we would otherwise lose over time, as well as releases signals that cause neurons to grow new connections. This makes sense if you think about the sea squirt anecdote once more. Our brain is the most metabolically demanding organ in our body. Much of that organ is devoted to our ability to generate movement.J6 If we don't move, much of our brain is less active too. Am I telling you that we must exercise just to maintain the brain capacity we have? Indeed I am. Exercise— provided it is of suficient intensity—makes us cognitively resilient. The benefits of exercise to brain health and neuroplasticity turn out to be robust at every age, for women, for men, for people vulnerable to age-related cognitive decline, and for both neurologically healthy and unhealthy people alike. Resistance training and cardiovascular training both impart huge benefits, but their combination (typically in separate workouts) turns out to be the most effective stimulus for brain health and neuroplasticity.J-Z And when mobility and flexibility, and walking, are added in, the positive results increase significantly. Some of the effects of exercise on brain health and neuroplasticity are the result of something called brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, a protein our brain makes that can exert a powerful role on learning and memory by virtue of its ability to sculpt and reinforce new neural circuit connections. Numerous studies have found that exercise leads to elevated levels of BDNF in the brainp These elevations are temporary,20 but enough to open the window for neuroplasticity for several hours after the exercise has ceased. Exercise also increases the release of catecholamines:gu that dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine trio that we discussed in the chapter on sleep and that we Will revisit throughout this book. When that trio is deployed in the body and brain, our levels of alertness and focus are increased, allowing us to access the memories, skills, and cognitive abilities we harbor in our neural circuits. As neuromodulators, the catecholamines also can Another way that exercise supports our brain and body is that it markedly improves sleep quality and duration.24 Remember from chapter 1: Morning workouts appear to shorten the amount of time it takes to fall asleep at night, and regular exercise has been found to improve the overall quality of sleep for adults. In a study including forty-eight adults with insomnia, moderate aerobic exercise improved sleep, and helped the participants feel less stressed.25 One caveat. If exercise is very intense and done too close to your desired bedtime, it can be detrimental to sleep. (We cover this more in chapter 1 and chapter 3.) It's best to either avoid intense exercise in the hours prior to sleep, or if you can't, to make sure you engage in some deliberate downregulation practices, such as a few minutes of long-exhale breathing or a hot shower, so that it does not negatively impact your sleep. There are many reasons Why appropriately timed exercise improves sleep. As discussed in chapter 1, the chemical adenosine, which not only builds up in the brain and body throughout the day but is also further increased with exercise, creates an increasing pressure to sleep.2 So exercise helps promote great sleep and reduces factors that lead to poor sleep. Regular physical activity also appears to increase the amount of time we spend in restorative slow-wave deep sleep, regardless of what time of day we exercise, and that translates to us feeling more rested when we wake. Then there is the benefit of moderate to intense exercise on our subjective waking experience, specifically on our feelings of well-being. Although "well-being" might sound nonscientific, for a lot of people it's an important barometer they use to gauge their quality of life. People who don't like exercise often look at me askance when I say that exercise improves mood, and not just because it helps us sleep better. But it's true: Exercise makes us happy. And relaxed.29 A moderate to intense workout is a proven, excellent way to snap ourselves out of a slump. Exercise reduces our baseline levels of stress, 1 increases our capacity to show resilience in a Wide range of circumstances,3— and reduces anger.3.3 These mood enhancements of exercise come from several different chemicals: dopamine, which increases motivation, focus, energy, and cognitive function; and serotonin, which does many things, including help make us more resistant to challenges. And here's a fun fact: The lactate your body produces during high-intensity exercise can physically modify—or lactylate—proteins in the brain, altering how neurons communicate. A recent study found that lactate production spurred by exercise reduced anxiety-related behaviors in mice, apparently by supporting the molecular machinery present at synapses between neurons in the prefrontal cortex. The prefrontal cortex has many parts and functions, but Will come up repeatedly in this book in the context of reducing impulsivity, decreasing anxiety, and learning new information and skills.3é There's more. Exercise has a surprising effect on our energy levels. The relationship between exercise and energy is key to understand, especially for those who feel they don't have the energy to exercise. After all, exercise requires energy, right? Right. For those who don't enjoy it or who have a ton of demands on their schedule and may not be sleeping well or enough, that's especially true. Add in a bit of low-level or major depression, anxiety about finances or the state of the world, or challenges with relationships in your life and, voila: You have a person who quite understandably does not want to exercise, and very likely won't exercise, no matter how many studies about its benefits or inspirational tales they see and hear. If this is you or someone you know, I hope what I'm about to share Will help. Yes, exercise requires energy to initiate and to complete, but it also gives us energy. I'm not just referring to energy in the psychological sense. I mean it gives us actual chemical energy and it does so by changing the electrical state of your nervous system. Work from neuroscientist Peter Strick's laboratory, at the University of Pittsburgh, identified three sets of brain areas that, when activated, communicate with our adrenal glands to cause them to release adrenaline.3Z In turn, this adrenaline activates receptors on our vagus nerve, which is a dense neural pathway that bidirectionally connects our body and brain. Our vagus nerve then triggers the release of norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus, which in turn can increase release of dopamine, acetylcholine, and other neuromodulators in other brain centers.3-g Other research found that exercise enhances a group of neurons in the hypothalamus—known as VMH SFI neurons— whose activity is required in order for endurancespecific adaptations to occur. Meaning, the brain is what actually coordinates the specific years of tracking physical activity and the causes of death of nearly seventeen thousand people between the ages of thirty-five and seventyfour.40 They found that the more a person walked, climbed stairs, or played sports, the less likely they were to die of heart disease. And the correlation was linear: The more physically active someone was, the lower the risk. This connection existed regardless of smoking status, weight, or having a parent who'd died young (a potential indicator of an inherited condition). The report, led by noted epidemiologist Ralph Paffenbarger, MD, and published in the New England Journal of Medicine, was considered a landmark—proof that exercise improved longevity, largely by preventing cardiovascular illnesses. Research since confirms this finding. In one study, researchers followed 3,307 people with heart disease from 1985 to 2014.41 Everyone in the study had been encouraged to exercise and lose weight. After thirty years, the researchers could see that while weight loss alone did not reduce the risk of death, exercise did. Other data confirm exercise's significance, even when people have other risk factors. One group of researchers 42 "Low described this link starkly, back in 1996. fitness is an important precursor of mortality," they wrote. To put that in Plain language: People who aren't active are more likely to die young. One mechanism behind this link is increased insulin sensitivity.43 Insulin is a hormone made and released from your pancreas that is essential for keeping your blood sugar, or glucose, levels within a particular range. Almost every cell in the body, including our neurons, requires glucose to function. Glucose comes from the food we eat and stored sources of energy, such as glycogen in our muscles and liver and adipose tissue, what is commonly referred to as body fat. Resistance to insulin leads to a buildup of glucose in our blood, which damages the endothelial cells that make up our capillaries, veins, and arteries, and deprives all cells of the glucose they need, impairing their functioning. It thus can cause cardiovascular disease and cerebrovascular diseases such as stroke and dementia. Exercise increases insulin sensitivity and can even improve the expression of genes that regulate insulin and glucose over long time spans which means more stable energy levels and reduced cellular inflammation and other symptoms of metabolic disorders. People with diabetes are more sensitive to insulin after exercising, too, and nondiabetics derive additional benefits from exercise-induced insulin sensitivity. Such benefits can be seen even after just one moderate workout. What's more, exercise can make your muscles become much better at pulling glucose out of the bloodstream, which ultimately helps your body handle carbohydrates more emciently.4.6 Finally (although I could go on!), there's this: As you now know from everything you've just read, exercise can make you healthier and happier, and it can allow you to get smarter too. It Will also extend your life. Your legs have quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves—each of which has its own subdivisions. You do two to three exercises for each of these groups. It's crucial that at least one of the two to three exercises for a muscle group be a compound (multi-joint) exercise. In most cases you'll also want to do one isolation (single joint) exercise for the same muscle group. Doing two to three exercises (with two to three work sets for each exercise) brings you to four to nine work sets per muscle group. (I recommend not going above nine work sets total for a single muscle group in a workout, given that you are training multiple muscle groups in each workout. Indeed, aiming for Six hard work sets per muscle group per workout is often better, provided that at least three of those sets are from a compound exercise and you take those work sets to failure.) Time constraints Will often dictate exactly how much you do. So Will how well you slept (I suggest aiming for the lower end of the number of sets on days when you are a bit sleep-deprived, but Still doing the compound movements). So Will nutrition. And stress. If you're well rested, fed, and you have the time, do the full three exercises for tvvo to three work sets each, for Six to nine total work sets. Or just do four to Six work sets per muscle group total and pour every bit of focus and energy into those. With time, you'll learn when enough is enough for that muscle group on a given day and according to the context of the rest of your life. Specific exercise selection: As mentioned earlier, target a muscle group with at least one compound exercise and one isolation exercise for that same muscle group. (I provide a set of video tutorials and options to select from at protocolsbookcom/videos). The rationale for including one of each is that compound exercises target a given muscle in conjunction with other muscles that it normally works with in various everyday movements. That also means compound movements allow you to use heavier weights, which provide not just a direct effect on the muscles you're training but also a positive "systemic effect" on various hormones and neurotransmitter systems of the brain and bodyg-6 And because they mimic a lot of pushing, pulling, kneeling, and lunging movements we do in everyday life, compound movements carry over to "real world" strength. The ones done standing, like squats and dead lifts, overhead presses, and even bicep curls or overhead extensions, help in developing more core stability and strength too. Taken to failure for two to three well-controlled, focused sets per muscle group, compound exercises are great... but they are pretty taxing on your nervous system. This is especially important considering you are doing at least one such movement, and perhaps even two, per muscle group, and training multiple muscle groups per workout. Follow with an isolation exercise for each major muscle group. It lets you intensely target a specific muscle, it reinforces the mind-muscle connection to that muscle, and, because of the mechanics of the movement (the position and range of motion, etc.), isolation exercises tend to develop aspects of the target muscle that compound movements may not target as thoroughly. And they don't create quite as much overall stress on your nervous system. Yes, exerciseinduced stress is good (!) but it adds up and, as stated earlier, you have just one nervous system for both your workouts and for the other aspects is of course also a factor. Again, the video links I provide give you lots of options. In the meantime, let's discuss the "best exercise" myth. The "best exercise/movement" myth Barbell squats (where the bar is on your shoulders as you squat down and stand up again) are a terrific compound exercise many people can and should use to target their quadriceps, glutes, and other leg muscles. They challenge your lower back and core muscles too. Some trainers Will say that you absolutely must do them, but that's simply not true. Some people have hip, leg, or shoulder mechanics that prevent them from doing barbell back squats without joint pain during the exercise or in the days after. You could work with a trainer to overcome those issues, but you could also substitute front squats, where the bar is held on the front of your shoulders, or hack machine squats, which have your back on an angled sled for support, or even leg presses for your quadriceps instead. There are Zercher squats, rear-leg-elevated squats, and goblet squats. There are also a near-endless number of lunge variations that target the quadriceps, glutes, and other muscles emphasized in the barbell back squat. The internet is filled with exercise clips showing all of these exercises. Again, I provide video tutorials of many to choose from at protocolsbookcom/videos. Find the exercises you can really push yourself in, without joint pain. You'll enjoy it more, and your results Will be greater... which Will lead you to enjoy it even more. You'll experience a whole different relationship to resistance training ifyou make yourself the CEO of the process. Only do exercises that really work for your body. Just don't only do isolation movements. Compound movements are necessary to get the full benefits of resistance training. A few quick notes about safety and pain Safety: 1'11 be direct about this. Be careful as you train. Done correctly (warm up, don't add more weight than you can handle with control, and so on) and with caution to avoid a few potentially perilous mistakes, resistance training as described in this protocol is a very safe activity. What sort of perilous mistakes am I referring to? Well, people have died barbell bench-pressingg-Z They couldn't push the bar up from their chest and they asphyxiated. It's rare, but it happens. Have a spotter who knows how to spot you correctly—which means they have to be strong enough to pull the loaded bar up off your chest or neck if need be. Ifyou don't have someone who can do that, an easy solution is to use dumbbells if you're benchpressing alone—those can be set down to your knees and dropped to your sides if you hit failure. A few dents in the floor are far better than the alternative. Or use a rack with safety pins (sturdy bars that can support a loaded bar) to set the weight on ifyou hit failure midrepetition. Same goes for barbell squats. Yes, you can "dump" the bar behind you if you hit failure, but far better to have a knowledgeable spotter. If no such person is around, again use a rack with pins so you can set the bar down and crawl out. Many people opt for machines like the leg press or hack squat for compound quadriceps movements for just this reason: It's easier to hit failure without doing what I described. And they usually have "stops" you can engage when you hit failure. No, these movements do not engage the same muscles to the same degree as free weight compound exercises. Yes, they are safer. You decide your risk tolerance, but be safe regardless. Also, think about your posture every time you are picking up or putting down weights, even if you're just replacing them on the rack or getting in position to start your set. A lot of resistance training injuries are the consequence of people not being mindful as they do the in-between work sets stuffbecause their mind is someplace else. I'm proud of the fact that I have been training hard, and heavy (for me) for nearly thirty-five years and have never had a serious injury from resistance training. (Knock on wood!) Sure, I've had a few minor strains here and there but nothing that floored me or kept me from training or daily activities for more than a few days. I attribute that to staying mentally focused from start to finish in the gym, and to only making relatively small incremental increases (5 to 10 percent) in the amount of weight I add to any given movement from week to week, and only once I can do at least eight to twelve reps of that movement in good form. Pain: We have all heard the mantra "no pain, no gain." News flash (!): That does not refer to joint or connective tissue pain. It refers to the burning sensation in muscles caused primarily by the accumulation of hydrogen ions inside muscle cells, brought on by the fact that the muscle cells need energy faster than oxygen can be delivered to them. (No, not lactic acid as was once believed. Lactate is created, but we know now it is not the cause of the burning.)ê-g If an exercise causes Sharp or dull joint pain—not post exercise soreness but, again, pain—either your form or the exercise itself is not right. Don't persist with that exercise. At least not that day. Find an alternative. REPETITION ("REPS") RANGE PER SET When it comes to selecting the number of reps to do for your work sets, you have options. After decades of debate about "optimal rep ranges," research from Brad Schoenfeld's lab, at Lehman College, found that using repetition ranges of anywhere from five all the way up to thirty on work sets stimulates essentially the same amount of hypertrophy. That is, if (and only if!) those sets are taken to failureg-2 Generally speaking, this is great news because it means that if you select a weight that you think you'll do eight reps with (and fail on rep nine) but somehow you are able to do eleven reps (and fail on rep twelve), you'll Still make progress. It removes the need to stay in a narrow rep range, at least for hypertrophy. At face value, these findings suggest you don't ever need to train with low reps and heavy weights to get results; you simply need to push until the final reps of your work set are very hard to complete. In some sense, yes, you can use moderate or even light weights (for you) that limit you to twelve to thirty reps before reaching failure. But you should also regularly use heavy (for you) weights, which means weights that limit you to just five to eight reps and no more, despite your maximum effort to complete more. Turns out using a mix of weights stimulates different muscle fiber types and ensures you activate different forms of cellular stress and thus adaptations. More on that below but in the meantime, if you don't want to have to think much about rep range selection, here's a good guide: For compound exercises, use the amount of weight on your work sets that has you reaching failure between five and twelve reps. • Occasionally use heavier loads that limit you to just 3—5 reps before you reach failure. • Experiment with lighter loads that allow you to complete higher repetition compound exercises, especially for quadriceps and calves. Many people find that 12—20 repetition squats (or its variations) are very effective for hypertrophy. • Warning: High-repetition quadriceps work sets taken to failure are brutal. The loads you use Will be lighter than you would use for 5—10 reps taken to failure, but the pain tolerance level on the final reps (and mental fortitude) required for 15—25 reps of a compound leg movement, like squats or even one of its machine variations, like a hack squat, taken to failure is no joke.

Still not convinced? Well, consider this reality: We all like to think we are training our absolute hardest, but what most people consider taking a set to failure almost always leaves one to two more repetitions in reserve. How can I be so sure? Well, if you hit failure on the eighth rep of a set but were told that getting a ninth rep would save someone's life, I am willing to bet that ninth rep would happen. So failure is somewhat subjective. Thankfully lives are not on the line according to when we reach failure on our lifts. But that momentary muscular failure is the closest thing you have to an objective measure of intensity of effort. So seek it out. Here's a bit more information so you can make the best-informed decisions about whether to train heavy, moderate, or light (for you). Hypertrophy adaptations are thought to be stimulated by at least three things: 1 Microdamage caused to the muscles using heavier loads. (Here, we can define "heavier loads" as sets that have you fail after completing three to Six reps.) The extent to which this contributes to hypertrophy is a matter of emerging debate, but it Still has some solid evidence in its favor. 2 Mechanical tension (from moderate to heavy loads and/or the contraction or stretching of the target muscle). 3 Metabolic stress (including the pump and cellular swelling, all brought on by enhanced blood flow, along with the release and delivery of various cellular factors to the muscles you are training).

Muscle size and strength are correlated so if you make a muscle bigger it Will get stronger, but training specifically to maximize strength is typically done by using loads that limit you to three to five reps (or fewer) and doing a large number of sets for each muscle across the week and not training to failure on any one set. Getting strong is great but the vast majority of people who resistance train do so to get stronger and for aesthetic changes that are best brought about by the rep and load ranges discussed above. That is Why I suggest you mainly use five to twelve reps on your compound work sets, and occasionally venture into using heavier loads that limit you to just three to five reps before you fail. In reality there Will be times when you can do ten reps of a movement with a given weight, so you increase the amount of weight the next time you're training that body part and somehow you can only do three or four reps before you reach failure. Don't worry about it. Just keep striving to add more reps or weight each workout in great form. If you want to obsess over something useful, obsess over the amount of focused effort you put into your work sets and using great form! About ten years ago, I decided to train exclusively with heavy weights that limited me to three to five reps on compound exercises and Six to ten reps on isolation exercises—which is called periodization. I did that for three months and I got a lot stronger, such that when I went back to doing five to twelve reps, I was stronger on every movement. Later I ran a similar experiment using lighter weights and more reps (12—25) for a few months... all Still to failure on work sets of course. I made considerable progress in terms of hypertrophy, but when I went back to using heavier weights for lower reps, I found I had Iost a lot of ground. So I learned something. Nowadays I almost always train with weights that limit me to five to twelve reps and only venture up to fifteen to twenty for an especially intense leg workout or on certain upper body isolation exercises. That's what is best for me and my goals. You should experiment and find what is best for you. Progressive overload is key! I know that the requirement for progressive overload is a giant "duh" to many of you out there, but others may need this reminder. If you do the same workout every week, using the same weights, reps, and sets, take note. You might sweat, work hard, and feel the mood enhancements of exercise but your progress Will halt. Because we're keeping the work sets to just two or three, you must challenge your muscles by either increasing the amount of weight or the number of reps, or both, while keeping your form excellent. "More weight or more reps, perfect form, and pushing to failure." That should be your resistance training mantra! Be aware that it's unreasonable to expect to add weight while maintaining the same rep count you performed the previous week, but it Will happen. Those are great workouts. However, there Will be weeks when, for whatever reason, you are not able to hit your target weight and rep goals in the gym. Consider the reasons: Are you sleep-deprived? Underfed, under caffeinated? Unfocused? Life happens, so don't obsess about it. Just do your absolute best for that day. If you find you're not making progress for two weeks in a row, you may need to reduce the set volume. Yes, I said it: Try doingfewer work sets and see if that budges you forward. Or maybe it's time for a week off to rest, so you can come back stronger. Finally, while IRM lifts and even 2RM lifts are great for building strength (and allow you to answer the "How much can you bench?" question you'll invariably get at some point), I recommend most people avoid doing IRMs. They come with too much risk of injury. If you really want to do them, fine, but use a spotter, please! And understand that IRM lifts are what you train for in powerlifting—which is a specific sport. If that's what you're interested in, there are great programs out there for powerlifting. But most people are lifting weights for other reasons. They want the variety of benefits that come from the resistance training I've described here. If someone ever asks me how much I can bench, I usually just tell them what I did for five to eight reps the preceding week because that's all I know for certain! An important note about training to, and past, failure As I've said about a hundred times now (but Still a hundred fewer than Mentzer would have in the same time frame!): Do the first work set of an exercise to failure, using perfect form. Pour everything you have into that set, on every repetition. That means, as the final reps approach, think: "This is what stimulates the adaptations I'm here for." Strive to keep your form stricter, and stress the targeted muscles more, not less as failure approaches. Then, when the weight won't reps, make sure they don't jump in before you reach failure. Make sure they force you to do the work. It's a fine line between spotting someone to ensure they don't get stuck in a dangerous position during a lift and getting someone to help you with forced reps. Spotting someone in the weight room is a skill —it's not brain surgery but there is a right and a wrong way to do it. On social media, you often come across videos of gym disasters, where people get stuck under the bench press or squat bar because they were too Shy to ask for a spot. There are, however, a nearly equal number of gym disaster videos of young kids who were not able to pull the bar off their dad's chest because they are too weak. Avoid all of this by making sure anyone you ask to help you is ( 1 ) strong enough to help with the arnount of weight you're using and (2) understands that you need to do the majority of the work. They are there to help keep you safe (again, especially on bench presses or squats where getting stuck can be dangerous), but not hinder your progress. Tell them: "1'11 let you know when to help but don't touch the weight until I say." And if they check their Phone during your work sets, find a new training partner! REST DURATION BETWEEN SETS Just as I listed above, take one to two minutes off between warm-up sets, and two to five minutes between work sets, depending on repetition range. Typically, people rest longer (3—5 minutes) between work sets of compound exercises than between work sets of isolation exercises (90 seconds to 3 minutes). Some people adhere to the clock for between set rest, others go by feel. You decide. I use the clock to get a sense of how my subjective "Okay, I'm ready for another set" sense matches up with various time ranges. Just don't talk, text, or scroll too much between sets. Stay focused, get the training done and get out. Recovery tips Then there's the rest that comes after your resistance training session. Great things happen for your health during your resistance training sessions but the really big benefits—the actual changes in your muscles, connective tissues, and brain—occur during the two to four days afterward, mostly while you sleep.93 The protocols provided elsewhere in this book Will help you get your sleep right and your nutrition and stress control right—all of which support recovery from, and adaptation to, exercise. You do not need to overhaul your sleep schedule or diet just because you resistance train. It is true that if you do a particularly hard workout, you may find you need a bit more sleep on subsequent nights, but in general, resistance training has the effect of improving the quality of your sleep, not increasing your sleep duration needs. Same with nutrition. Resistance training doesn't massively change your nutritional needs. Assuming you are already eating in the manner I describe in chapter 4—meaning you strive to eat about 1 gram of quality protein per pound of lean body weight daily, as well as plenty of vegetables, some fruit, unprocessed starches, and healthy fats. that if you are actively seeking to It is true gain muscle, you'll need to eat more calories than you burn each day, but not by much—200 to 400 calories more than your maintenance calories is fine.24 The old-school practice of bulking up by eating many more calories than you need is just not healthy—and brings with it a lot of body fat that you'll be trying to lose later.25 1 suggest you don't go that route. Provided you are not undernourished in calories or protein, you'll make progress with resistance training. Keep in mind as you gain more muscle and/or lose fat, your caloric needs change—fortunately in a way that lets you eat the same or more while staying lean or even getting leaner. Muscle tissue is metabolically demanding, which means it burns more calories than fat tissue, which is just one of the many benefits of resistance training. There is a formula for determining your maintenance calorie needs per day, or what is called your basal metabolic rate (BMR). That's how many calories you should eat each day to maintain your current body weight if you did no physical activity whatsoever. The formula is called the Katch-McArdle formula.26 It takes about five minutes to figure out, and it's very easy to do. It requires a few other simple calculations first, which 1'11 walk you through. Determine your body weight (BW) in kilograms: • The formula uses kilograms so ifyou're used to thinking about weight in pounds and not kilograms, first divide your body weight (BW) in pounds by 2.2 to get your weight in kilograms.

• Very active (eg., walking 7K—10K steps, effortful resistance training or cardio): BMR x 1.725 • Extremely active (eg., same as very active but twoa-day-workouts): BMR x 1.9 1'11 add one comment on estimating your activity levels from sports performance expert Andy Galpin. Based on his experience training hundreds of clients in reaching their fitness goals, Andy notes that people are typically far less active than they think. For example, most who rate themselves "very active" are actually moderately active. He recommends that people select the activity category below the one they think they fall into if they're interested in losing weight. I don't do resistance training and cardio on the same days, but I try to get seven thousand to ten thousand steps in every day, and I resistance train three times a week and do some form of cardio three days a week. Occasionally, I Will resistance train or run, and then also go for a hike. That constitutes extremely active but it's too rare an occurrence. Also, given Andy's recommendation, 1'11 consider myself "very active" and therefore multiply my basal metabolic maintenance calories (2,314 calories) by 1.725 = 3,991.65 calories. andl round that up to 4,000 calories per day. I naturally tend to eat less on days I don't exercise, so for that day, I multiply 2,314 by 1.3 75 = 3,181.75 calories. Voila! I need about 4,000 calories per day on my training days and about 3,000 calories per day on my non-training days. Do I neurotically count every calorie? No. Truth be told, I probably eat about 3,500 calories on training days, and about 3,000 calories on days I don't train. Should you count calories? Maybe, but not every day and certainly not forever. I suggest figuring out your basal metabolic maintenance calories, what you're consuming now, and what changes you need to make, and then Stick to that revised plan most of the time. After you've completed the simple formula above, a great tool to track what you're eating is the Carbon app developed by Layne Norton, PhD, who is an expert in training and nutrition. (Carbon is a sponsor of my podcast because I believe it to be a terrific product.) Another option is the Cal A1 app. Both make it very easy to enter what you eat and the apps then do all the calculations of calories, as well as macronutrients like protein, fats, and carbohydrates. Each carries a nominal cost, but it is very easy to use. Personally, I don't like to count calories every day, but I use the Carbon app for periods of time to see how I'm doing. If you want to lose weight, eating 300 to 500 fewer calories than you burn daily is the best way to go. By resistance training while in this caloric deficit, you're better able to spare lean muscle and preferentially lose fat.2Z This is further helped by making sure you're eating a protein-rich diet, despite eating 300 to 500 fewer calories. In short, resistance training and a good diet are two of the most effective and durable paths to body recomposition—a fancy term for "gaining muscle and losing fat," as opposed to simply losing weight.

Pre-training and post-training nutrition: I prefer to resistance train early in the morning or midafternoon, and I consistently have my best workouts when I have not eaten anything in the hours before I begin. I like to wake up, get sunlight, hydrate, caffeinate, then train, and then eat afterward, but some people just can't do that. They feel weak, tired, hungry, or nauseous if they train on an empty stomach. But I know myself well. If 10:00 or 11:00 am. rolls around and I haven't eaten, I need to ingest some calories before training. That's usually a few scoops of whey protein, a small bowl of oatmeal, a piece of fruit, and some nuts. Nothing fancy. Or two to three eggs, instead of the whey. You'll have to experiment to see what works best for you. If you eat before you train, ideally give yourself at least an hour to digest your food before you begin. After resistance training, your body is primed to convert any food you consume into energy to burn at a very high rate, so it can replace glycogen you used during the workout.98 That does not mean you should gorge on pastries or pizza after training. Unless you're deliberately low-carb or keto, the meal following a resistance training workout ideally should include both natural sugars (a few pieces of fruit) and starchy complex carbohydrates (such as rice, potatoes, bread, pasta, or oatmeal) to replenish glycogen stores in your liver and muscles. It should also include some quality protein (such as whey, beef, chicken, fish, turkey, or eggs). This meal doesn't have to be complicated. The enzymes that facilitate restocking of glycogen are upregulated after resistance training,22 and you five to ten grams of creatine monohydrate daily, as a powder dissolved in water. You can take it any time of day, with or without food. Any reputable brand with third-party testing and that is "Certified for Sport" is fine. I have seen no evidence that creatine harms your kidneysJ-Q4 or makes your hair fall out,l-O-5 which is what some online claims say. It's normal to gain a few pounds of water-in-the-muscles weight with regular creatine use. If you stop taking it, you urinate out that extra fluid. Whey protein is simply a high-quality, easily digested protein. It's convenient and cost-effective when compared to other quality proteins. It doesn't have many other micronutrients like meat or eggs do, however, so I wouldn't make whey protein your only quality protein source. I drink one to two scoops of whey protein mixed with water once or twice a day, which equates to 20 to 80 grams of protein (it's about 20 g of protein per scoop). Along with the foods I eat, this helps me meet my daily protein goal. Without whey protein I find it challenging to eat about 1 gram per pound of lean body weight each day. The other supplement worth mentioning in the context of resistance training is caffeine, which has been shown to improve exercise performance when 100 to 400 milligrams is consumed about thirty minutes prior to and even during exercise. 106 That's about one to four cups of coffee, depending on the brew strength and size of the serving. Not everyone can or should consume caffeine, however. It makes some people anxious. I personally love caffeine and tolerate it very well, so I drink a cup or two of black coffee and/or a yerba maté about thirty minutes before resistance workouts. A lot of people are into energy drinks these days as pre- and intra-workout energy sources. I Will occasionally drink an energy drink (Jocko Go or Gorilla Mind—l know, wild names!—are the ones I like best for taste and effect) before and during a workout, but not every time. If I am facing a particularly challenging leg workout I tend to make my own pre-workout by drinking (or taking) 200 milligrams of caffeine and alphaGPC (300—900 mg). I discuss alpha-GPC and other compounds more in chapter 6. Just remember, if you're working out in the evening, drinking caffeine beforehand Will really disrupt your sleep. There are a few other supplements which have been shown to improve exercise performance— like Rhodiola rosea, which can reduce fatigue during training, 1 7 but I consider it a distant fourth place to the three mentioned already. But I want to reiterate: You do not need supplements to make progress resistance training. Focus on training properly! Then focus on recovery, meaning letting the adaptations you stimulated in the gym actually occur by getting proper sleep and nutrition. That is what really moves the needle. A week off every twelve to sixteen (or even ten to twelve) weeks: I attribute taking a week off from resistance training every three to four months or so as one of the main reasons I have been able to make regular progress in resistance training over the last thirty-five years. I know that sounds crazy, and that it runs counter to much of the "no days off" advice seen online, but I am convinced it's the way to go, for three reasons. First, it gives your joints and your mind a chance to reset. Any nagging aches or residual muscle soreness tend to go away during that week off, and you come back feeling reset. Second, most people make actual progress during the week off Training-induced stress is cumulative; when we train and recover between workouts, we get stronger and can manage more reps and/or more weight in perfect form from week to week, but not all our bodily tissues adapt at the same rate. By the time we are eight, nine, or even fourteen weeks into training since our last week off, we tend to have a harder time recovering from workouts. Taking a week off lets everything catch up, and lets you come back stronger. Third, it's common that after twelve to sixteen weeks of training we feel less motivated to keep training hard. The relatively low frequency of resistance training I recommend in this program —just three times per week—usually staves off boredom but some people do start to lose steam after ten or more weeks of training. If you find yourself dragging yourselfto the gym, and you're more interested in texting than training once you're there, take a week off, and come back. That usually does the trick. You'll be more energetic when you do. Keep in mind, too, that sometimes we are just forced to take a week off because life says we have to! I don't think training when you're sick is a good idea, and it gets others sick, too, so please stay out of the gym until you're better! Other times we are forced to take a week off because we have a major deadline or a family vacation or other demands. I personally like to train on vacations because it helps me get over jet lag when I travel, but you may feel like it's a waste of time. It's a matter of choice, and how you View vacation. Regardless of whether your week off is due to a cold or pre-planned for the end of a twelve to sixteen week stretch of training, or simply because a work deadline hits, don't worry about it causing a setback. It's part of the process. Just get back to training (properly) after that week off.
