In the meantime, know that you have a fair degree of flexibility, and you can move a workout forward or back a day if needed. Can I Still play sports and do other activities? Of course. You'll be stronger for it. And the relatively low volume of sets in this program means you won't be sore all the time. (Again, soreness is zero indication of an effective workout —it does not mean you effectively stimulated specific hypertrophy or strength adaptations.) Please don't add additional resistance training work or CrossFit workouts and the like until you've tried this program, but tennis, Pilates, hiking, yoga, archery, golf, soccer, et cetera, and being active with house and yard work is encouraged. Most people nowadays are too sedentary. More movement is nearly always better than less. And of course, cardiovascular training is key. I discuss that next.
EXERCISE PROTOCOL Do Cardiovascular Training Three Times per Week
WHAT TO DO

• Elevate your heart rate for anywhere from Six to seventy-five minutes, three times per week. Plan three sessions, each focused on stimulating a different specific adaptation: a long, a medium, and a brief cardiovascular workout, scaling the intensity inversely with the duration of each session. That means the long cardio workout should be of low intensity, the brief cardio workout should be ofhigh intensity. Here is how to incorporate cardio into the overall program: Day 1: Cardiovascular training, 45—75 minutes (IOW intensity/long duration) Day 2: Resistance training (legs: calves, quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes) Day 3: Rest day Day 4: Resistance training (torso: chest, back, abdominals/core; optional neck) Day 5: Cardiovascular training, 25—30 minutes (moderate intensity/moderate duration) few minutes to that each week, until you're doing forty-five to seventy-five minutes of continuous movement. In my observation, most people find that Sixty minutes is about the upper limit of their psychological tolerance for this sort of exercise, unless they really love the activity or it's made social, like a hike or bike ride with family or friends. In any case, your goal pace throughout should be such that you can just barely hold a conversation. It's quite all right if you must pause your speech here and there to catch your breath, but the idea is to exert yourself at a level that, were you to push yourself any faster or harder, holding a conversation would be impossible. Another way to calibrate to that goal pace is to push as hard as you can while Still breathing in and out only through your nose. No mouth breathing whatsoever, unless you are talking. As soon as you feel you have to gasp to get air through your mouth, you know you're pushing too hard. In the language of percentage of maximum heart rate this cardio session is done at 60 to 70 percent of your maximum heart rate (HR), but ideally closer to 70 percent. Your max HR can be estimated by this formula: 220 — your age = your approximate max HR. That's not a perfect measurement but it's close, and for most it's more than suficient to use here. If you want to be more precise about it, max HR is better approximated by the following formula: for men, you take 208 beats per minute — (0.7 x your age in years); and for women, it's 206 beats per minute — (0.88 x your age in years).m Once you have determined your approximate max HR, multiply that by 0.6 and 0.7 to get the lower and upper range, respectively, of your target heart rate for this cardio session. I've shared this formula because some people like to use an HR monitor while training to be sure they stay in that target HR zone. I prefer to use the "upper limit of effort while maintaining nasal breathing" approach, because whenever I have measured my HR while running and restricting myself to nasal breathing, it lands at about 70 percent (+/—5 percent) ofmy max HR. I have nothing against HR monitors. I just prefer not to use one when doing this workout. I like to let my mind wander or to listen to a book or podcast or music but if you like tracking your HR in real time, go for it. A few other things to consider for this workout: Some people refer to this as Zone 2 cardio, which is a term that describes the intensity of the exercise with regard to heart rate training zones. But on that scale, I consider it more Zone 2/3 because it's done at the high end of Zone 2 and the low end of Zone 3 Ideally you would get outside to do this workout so that you're getting all the benefits that come with being outdoors. This raises the issue of what type of exercise is best for this. That's an easy one to answer. Select any activity you can do for the specified duration and intensity without getting hurt. That means do what is safe for your joints, works for your skill level, doesn't stress any of your injuries, and can be completed in safe conditions. I love running and much prefer doing it outside on a trail or City streets to all other forms of cardio, but many people loathe running, or it hurts their knees, or it's not safe for them to run in a given area. You don't have to run! You can opt for cycling, or use the elliptical machine or a stair climber, or hike with a weight vest or a rucksack or, heck, even a backpack with a onegallon jug of water in it. The possibilities are nearly infinite, and many of these cost very little. If I don't run, 1'11 sometimes swim laps in a pool or swim parallel to shore in the ocean. Ifthe weather is bad, 1'11 occasionally run on a treadmill or use a stationary bike. Pick your poison and deliver it Slow and steady for forty-five to seventy-five minutes. Many people find this workout meditative and learn to enjoy it. While you can of course go longer than seventy-five minutes, remember you're training your legs the next day. The second cardio workout each week iS done three days after your leg workout (day five of the program). By then, your legs should be feeling mostly or completely recovered. This second cardio workout should be moderately fast-paced. It should have you breathing fairly hard but not gasping for air or needing to stop to recover. I suggest you start with five minutes of lowintensity movement to warm up and then shift to twenty-five to thirty minutes of "work" where your heart rate is kept between about 75 and 85 percent of your maximum heart rate. Using the heart rate training zones, this workout falls in the high Zone 3 and low Zone 4 range. Notably, although this workout is more intense than the first cardio session, it generally leaves you feeling energized and focused for many hours afterward. The key is to not push overly hard at any one time of that approximately twenty-five to thirty minutes. You want to stay roughly in that "75 to 85 percent of max HR" range. That There are many ways to do max heart rate training but the total time spent at near-all-out effort is always pretty brief: as short as about Six minutes, and up to about sixteen minutes. Either works for this third cardio session. What form of exercise you choose can vary. For example, you could hop on an assault bike —those stationary bikes with a fan and handles that you pump forward and back while you pedal. You'll soon realize that the fan is there to increase the resistance, not just to cool you down. Or you could use a stationary bike that lets you adjust the resistance of the pedals. You could also go sprint at a track or on a trail, or swim in a pool. The important thing is to do something in which you can really exert yourself without getting injured. A "fun" HIIT session is this: brief five- to tenminute warm-up, then pedal (or run, row, or swim, etc.) as hard and fast as you can for thirty seconds, then rest or Slow down for Sixty seconds, then another thirty seconds of all-out effort, then back again to Sixty seconds of rest or low effort, and so on, for a total of Six to twelve rounds of alternations. I do this on the assault bike once a week. I love-hate it. You Will quickly realize that with each round of all-out effort it gets tougher and tougher to recover, such that by rounds Six to twelve, those Sixty seconds of rest Will seem to go by extremely fast. There is actually a neuroscientific basis for the warping of time perception we experience under stress that I discuss in the next chapter. The good news is, even though this workout is intense, the whole thing, including the warmup, only takes about twenty-five minutes. At the end, you Will feel fatigued, but remarkably, within five to ten minutes after stopping you Will likely feel extra energized from all the adrenaline and norepinephrine you generated in your body and brainll You Will also have provided a great stimulus to improve your V02 max, and max HR, the importance of which I cover below. Other options for this workout include the Cooper test, where you see how far you can go (run, swim, cycle, etc.) in twelve minutes of steady, hard effort.J-!5 That is a "fun" one too. Or you can try to run your best mile time. This is something performance coach, author, and former elite runner Steve Magness has emphasized as being a terrific correlate of V02 maxll It's one of my favorite workouts. Here is how to do it properly: First find a 400-meter track. Start by warming up with an easy jog of four to Six laps slowly interspersing the occasional faster-paced 100 meters—not all out but just quickening your pace to about 60 to 70 percent of your subjective "run for your life" speed. Perhaps do that on one straight-track segment between turns on each warm-up lap. Once you feel properly warmed up, run four laps (which is 1,600 meters—about 9 meters Shy of 1 mile). It's a skill to run the mile and pace everything just right for your best time. But you're not aiming to be a competitive miler here. So set out at a pace you can maintain for three laps—about 85 percent of "running for your life" speed, then push it harder on the last lap, or 95 percent of "running for your life" speed. The key is to pace yourself so you're not sprinting laps one to three and then forced to walk or jog the remainder. It can take a bit of practice but within a few weeks you'll know the pace to take for each lap. Almost everyone likes to really push the final 200 meters or sos I test my approximate best mile time about once every two months lately. I'm not training to be a competitive miler but it's nice to have one version of the short intense cardio workout where I can track my progress across the year. I doubt 1'11 beat my best time from high school ever again, but it's fun to have an "a bit faster than last month" run. My goal is to maintain or reduce my mile time each time I run it. And there is the Norwegian 4x4, if you want to try itu-Z That's where you warm up, and then run, bike, or row hard for four minutes, then rest or Slow down for four minutes. Repeat this cycle for a total of four work-rest rounds. As you can see with all these examples, the exact work-to-rest ratio and total time can vary dramatically, and yet all can be effective. What's key is that during the work periods, you're truly working hard. That is because, during the rest periods, you're allowing enough time for recovery so that you can again come back to a truly hard effort. Don't be overly caught up in the exact protocols. You can alter them if you like and Still get the same results. I'm recommending three different types of cardio training sessions every week because this variation is typically what delivers the best results over time for improving your V02 max. We're trying to balance duration and intensity in this program. It's best to emphasize both. You want longer moderate efforts and you want brief and very intense efforts. And while the shorter, intense efforts are extremely effective (and time eficient), they take longer to recover from stronger with low repetition heavy sets in the gym equates to you being able to move more weight on your higher repetition sets once you get stronger. So, while people often debate which form of cardiovascular exercise is best for overall health and longevity, that's not the lens through which to look at it. I suggest a practical lens. (And you know by now, I don't believe in any best type of exercise; only the best way to structure an effective exercise program.) For instance, consider that your one-mile time is a good reflection of your V02 max.123 Does that mean you should only do one mile distances for cardio? No. In fact, whether you're a competitive miler or simply using the one-mile time test as a fun workout and barometer of your V02 max, doing some longer/lower, moderate, and brief/high intensity cardio workouts across the week is how to get faster at the mile. In science we love to isolate variables, so people have done the "which cardio exercise is best?" experiment. That research made Clear that if you have to choose one type, you want to opt for brief/high intensity cardio rather than, say, three thirty- to forty-five-minute Zone 2/3 sessions.12 But doing a mix of durations and intensities is recommended, and for the reasons mentioned above, it meshes well with your resistance training. A Zone 2/3 jog or hike for an hour the day before you train your legs with weights is no problem. Sprinting the day after leg training to failure? Not a good idea. The injury risk is too high. Doing these three cardio training sessions also means you're logging a total of about two hours per week of cardio. Considering the immediate and long-term health benefits, that's a great return on investment. We hear all the time about "fitness" and it reflects many things. But from a health perspective consider that two studies—one published in 2018 and another in 2022—both showed essentially the same thing, which is that as you move from the lowest to the higher tiers of cardiorespiratory fitness (one measure of that is your V02 max), your mortality risk drops.125 These are meaningful shifts in life expectancy too. One of the studies states, "Those with the highest fitness had roughly five times lower mortality than the least fit." Resistance training is cardiorespiratory fitness, but less about its effects in maintaining (or increasing) muscle mass and bone density, promoting cognitive function and healthy body recomposition, make a combination of resistance training and cardio training two of the three vital interlocking puzzle pieces for excellent physical health.
COMMON QUESTIONS

Does doing three cardio training sessions per week prevent you from building muscle? And does resistance training harm my cardio efforts? To be clear: If your goal is purely to put on as much muscle as possible, or to do an endurance event like a half marathon or marathon as fast as possible, there are better training programs for those specific goals. When splitting your time across both building muscle and building endurance, there's going to be a performance trade-off. You can't maximize for both at the same time because of so-called interference effects.12 That said, for vitality, health, longevity, aesthetics, and all-around fitness, you want to do both resistance training and cardio training. Research indicates that the interference effects are minimal when done on separate days at the duration and intensities similar to those in this foundational program. 12 What if I play a sport? If you're training for a competition or a race, or you play a sport like soccer or tennis or basketball, and you play hard for an hour or more one to two times per week, the program here is Still great. You may want to do the lower number of work sets, and you'll really need to tend to your recovery and nutrition by making sure you get enough hours of quality sleep and calories— including, yes, enough quality protein, but also starches and fats. Again, the program here Will get you the most all-around fit as possible at any age. That does not mean you won't gain strength and muscle—you Will. You Will also burn fat. You'll increase your endurance too. And once you learn how different exercises impact your body, you can emphasize some and reduce others, per the suggestions I describe in this protocol. Exercise done correctly is very potent in that way. Assuming you pay attention to the points I make about recovery too—that is, eat well and sleep well—l'm certain you'll achieve remarkable results with this program. What if I haven't slept well, should I train or not?

If you are healthy, and you happen to have had a bad night's sleep—by which I mean only one to two hours less sleep than usual—then try to Stick with your workout. There is a growing amount of data that say it can help offset some of the shortterm cognitive disturbances from sleep loss. 12 Just be careful not to push too hard in the gym (or in life) after a poor night's sleep as injuries happen more often when people have not slept enoughl-?-2 And don't make it a regular thing to get less than enough sleep, and expect to remedy that with exercise. You'll end up sick, injured, or both. Maybe do some non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) (see Sleep Protocol 8) and then push through the workout. If you have had a really bad night's sleep for two or more nights in a row, for whatever reason, I suggest you get back on track with your sleep before exercising again. Consider some deliberate heat exposure (sauna or a hot bath, for example), and if you feel you must exercise, try a restorative activity, like stretching, light yoga, or just walking. Is it better to eat before or after training? There is no Clear rule here. Personally, I prefer to train in the morning on an empty stomach. Figure out what works for you. It may be best to eat prior to training if you wake up hungry and you know that hunger Will distract you during your workout, or you get dizzy or nauseous training on an empty stomach. Some people may find that eating about Sixty to ninety minutes prior to exercise gives them an energy boost without the discomfort of feeling full. It's highly individual. Experiment with your timing of your workouts and meals.

If I miss a day of cardio or resistance training, should I change the weekly schedule? It's hard to answer this one because. it depends. However, I would not change the order of your resistance or cardio training sessions across the week because the schedule starts to fall like dominoes, and it's hard to get back on track. But maybe something comes up and you can't do the long, Slow cardio day as planned. I would not recommend moving that workout to the same day you train legs. I would simply skip the long cardio day and train your legs on schedule. Skipping leg day is a bad idea. You do three days of cardio per week, so having to miss one every now and again is not a huge deal. But you only train your legs directly once a week, and done correctly as outlined above it creates major positive systemic shifts in your brain and body. So when people say, "Don't skip leg day," it's not just about aesthetics. In fact, if I could only train once per week in the gym and do one cardio training session—not what I recommend, but if I had to— I would do leg day and I would do some sprints followed by light jogging four or five days later. That's just to illustrate a point about the potency of those two workouts. I recommend the full program described in this chapter. Let's say you can't do the moderate cardio training session for whatever reason. You could, in theory, shift it to immediately after your arms workout that same day. But remember, you're scheduled to do the long, Slow cardio session the very next day, and you don't want your legs to feel like noodles when you wake up the following morning for leg day! So think ahead a bit about your recovery.
EXERCISE PROTOCOL Incorporate Brief Mobility and Flexibility Work Two to Four Times per Week
WHAT TO DO

• Do four specific movements to improve your mobility, two to four times a week. • Refer to the instructions below to target areas susceptible to injury as you do these movements. Wrist, back, knee, hip, and shoulder injuries are common. The movements described here Will ensure mobility in these areas. T hey aren't a guarantee against injuries, but they can help tremendously.
HOW IT WORKS

First, I'm not giving you yet another workout to do. The current program—about three hours a week of resistance training, about two hours of cardio—is not terribly time-consuming, considering the years (literally!) it can add to your life. Still, I acknowledge that people's time is Consider a stiff-legged deadlift or similar variation for your hamstrings, glutes, and lower back—the so-called posterior chain. It involves holding a barbell or dumbbells and moving from standing to something resembling a toe-touch (or an attempt to) by lowering the weight under control toward the ground, and then standing up again. You can imagine the stretch to your hamstrings and lower back that movement provides if you use a full range of motion. Including some movements that are most challenging for a given muscle group when it is in the elongated position can help build flexibility and can help you remain "strong in any position," which assists mobility too.1 1 Again, if any ofthis is confusing, I provide a gallery of movements to choose from at protocolsbookcom/videos. I also hope you'll include the direct mobility exercises that I describe below in your weekly routine but even if you don't, by training the way I describe above, most people Will improve their mobility, and flexibility too. We're talking about the ability to touch your toes while keeping your legs straight or just slightly bent, to hang from a bar with no pain, to twist around to look behind you while seated in a chair, to sit in a deep squat for one to two minutes (and be able to stand up at the end!), and so on. You can develop those basic abilities through resistance training with a full range of motion, and focusing on the relevant muscles at all positions in each rep. There are many great ways to improve mobility. Here I have created what I believe is the minimal effective dose of it. And if you want to do more mobility work, please do!

At least two to four times a week, take ten minutes and do the following four movements. You can do these most any place and at any time. 1 Deep sumo squat, torso twist, point, and look up Set your feet a few inches wider than your shoulders, then squat down as far as you can. Put your elbows against the insides of your knees and your palms and fingers together in "prayer" position, and push out gently with your elbows until you feel a stretch in your hips and inner thighs. Then raise one arm and, with your index finger, point directly up at the ceiling (or as high overhead as you can) while keeping your other elbow against the inside of your knee. Let your gaze follow your finger, which Will naturally have you twist your torso and turn your neck to raise that arm. Look directly up at your index finger for three to ten seconds. Inhale and exhale. Then put your arm down, reset to the first squat position with both elbows against the insides of your knees. Place your hands in prayer position for three to ten seconds, and then raise your other arm up to point at the ceiling. Twist your torso and look up at your index finger for three to ten seconds. Repeat three times for each side. You may have to stand up between sets. That is fine. This is a great movement because it gets you squatting deep, it improves your thoracic spine and neck mobility, and you'll also feel a decent stretch in your inner thighs and hips. It Will also reveal if you have any asymmetries in your mobility (perhaps one side versus the Other) which is common.

I demonstrate this protocolsbookcom/videos. movement here: Note: Ifyou can't point and/or look all the way up to directly overhead, start by pointing and looking up at a lower angle. Gradually progress to pointing and looking directly overhead. 2 Get your knees behind your glutes, one at a time This is one I learned from mobility expert Kelly Starrett whom I mentioned earlier in this chapter. Since it may not be easy for most people to envision, try this: Start in a standing lunge by placing one foot in front of you and the other foot behind you. Bend your front knee and keep your rear leg straight or a bit bent. Now nudge the foot in front of you slightly farther out. Bend that front knee more and focus on stretching the hip flexors at the top of your back leg. You may need to lean your torso back a bit to really feel the hip flexor stretch. Okay, notice the knee of your back leg is now behind your glutes? That is what I mean by "get your knee behind your glutes." Slowly ease into this hip flexor stretch for ten to thirty seconds while exhaling. It's fine to reach up and look overhead while doing this, as that Will help extend the hip flexor, but keep your attention on the back leg. Your front leg is there for stability and you can bend it to provide more rear-placed-leg hip stretch. Repeat for each side three times. I demonstrate this movement here: protocolsbookcom/videos. Next, you're going to kneel on both knees. Then put one knee up in front of you (the foot of that same leg is thus flat on the ground). The Shin of your rear leg is parallel to the ground. That means angle. Many people find they can't get into this "reverse tabletop" position for very long, if at all, but some can. See ifyou can hold that position for ten seconds. If you can't do this, practice doing this each week for three sets of however long you can hold it until you can easily remain in this position for ten seconds. Once you can do that, move to the following progression: Sit on the floor with your feet in front of you, with the soles of your feet and butt on the ground, and your knees bent. Place your hands just behind your hips, with your palms down. Turn your hands so your fingers point backward. See if you can slowly push your pelvis up so that the tops of your legs and torso are parallel to the floor, and your knees are at a 90 degree right angle. Once again, the goal is to get into the flat reverse tabletop position and hold for ten seconds. For some people this Will take a while to achieve. For others it Will be easy depending on your level of shoulder mobility. These movements are also great for wrist mobility, too, by the way. Once that final "reverse tabletop" variation is achievable, then you can start to experiment SLOWLY with this next movement. Sit on the floor with your legs straight in front of you, heels on the ground and the soles of your feet facing forward. Place your hands flat on the ground just behind you, with your fingers pointed backward. Keep them there as you gently and slowly scoot your glutes forward. Remember, your hands stay flat on the ground and fixed in place. Keep scooting forward until you feel a stretch in your biceps and shoulders. Exhale, and see if you can ease into it another centimeter or so. Once you can extend your shoulders back behind you with the edges of your hands touching, you are getting to quite mobile shoulder status. The reason to do this: Tight shoulders can arise from many sources, but often there Will be people who can raise their arms to the front or to the side without issue but who don't have the mobility to raise their arms up behind them, meaning they don't have much shoulder extension mobility. This is made worse by desk work, and the chin-down/forward-leaning posture that is nearly ubiquitous nowadays, thanks to excessive amounts of time texting and scrolling on our phones. Shoulder tightness and neck and back pain are often linked too. Improving your shoulder extension mobility is straightforward. It just requires a willingness to work through these progressions. Wrist, back, knee, hip, and shoulder injuries are super common and many can be avoided by a quality strength training program and by including some basic mobility exercises like the ones in this protocol. Some quick movements you can incorporate in your routine are the "face pulls," which strengthen these and other areas, as well as neck training a few times a week, as described in Exercise Protocol 2 and shown at protocolsbookcom/videos.You Will be amazed at how strong, mobile, and stable your shoulders, neck, and upper back Will be ifyou do. Do not push too fast when it comes to mobility work! Work through the progressions listed above over the course of months or more. Make it painless but deliberate, and you Will build and maintain much greater shoulder, hip, knee, back, and wrist mobility.

4 Practice the Founder pose The final mobility exercise is the Founder pose, made popular by chiropractor Eric Goodman, who has served as a conditioning coach for numerous top athletes in sports ranging from cycling to surfing to water POIO. I was referred to his work by friends who previously had back pain and shoulder pain, and who sit a lot of the day. "You have to try this thing called Founder pose," I kept hearing. Mind you, in my role, I hear that about a thousand times per day about a variety of things, so I'm not easily moved to try them. But I heard this decompresses the spine and trains your musculature to work properly as a functional unit. I tried Eric's Founder pose and, wow, it's great. Not just because it feels good while you do it but your posture improves. And it definitely made me more flexible. So what is it? It's similar to the "chair pose" in yoga but while that mainly emphasizes the musculature of the front of the body, the Founder pose emphasizes mobility of your posterior and lateral chains: your hamstrings, glutes, lower and upper back, and thoracic muscles. Here is how you do it: Stand with your feet a bit wider than your shoulders, toes pointing slightly out. Stand as tall as you can by pressing your heels down and lifting your head up, as if a string were tied to the top of your head but your heels were fastened down to the ground. Hinge your hips so you lean slightly forward at the waist—almost as though you're about to sit in a chair but freeze only about a third of the way down into the movement. Your hips and glutes are back behind your heels, and your knees are just slightly bent. Keep your head as far away from your glutes as possible. You should feel a stretch in your lower back and hamstrings. If not, lean farther forward at the waist until you do. Raise your chest, and with your arms at your sides, turn your thumbs out and away from the midline of your body (away from your belly button). Keeping your thumbs rotated out, start to slowly lift your arms. Stop when you feel more stretching in your lower back and/or the backs of your legs. Now move your hips back a few inches more. And raise your chest and head, aka "make your spine long," Still pressing your heels down. Raise your arms a bit more ifyou can (thumbs Still pointed away from your navel in external rotation), all the while pushing your heels down. Hold this position for five more seconds then stand up straight. Repeat that one to two times, as often as every day or even just a few times a week. Thank me later. No, thank Eric Goodman!
